objection: Your price is too high.
means: Almost never a final no. It usually means they don’t yet see enough value for the number, they’re comparing you to something cheaper, or they’re testing whether the price moves if they push.
avoid: Dropping the price in the first minute, or running to your manager. Both teach the buyer that pushing works, and both cost you margin you didn’t need to give.
steps: Agree that it’s a real number. Arguing makes people dig in.
Ask what they’re comparing it to: another offer, another product, or the budget in their head.
Separate the price from the product. If it’s the right fit, you’re working out a number together, not starting over.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. And thank you for shopping with us, because you could have gone anywhere. You didn’t walk off the lot, so I can tell you like it. Can I ask you a couple of questions? Too high compared to what? And if we got it to fit your budget, the way you’d like, would that be okay? All right, perfect. Let’s start there.”

variants.auto: “Thank you so much for sharing. Let’s make sure you love it first. Take it for a drive. Then we’ll make sure the numbers are on your terms.”
variants.insurance: “Thank you so much for sharing. Can I ask you a couple of questions? Let’s look at what’s driving the premium. We can adjust coverage, but let’s not cut the part that protects your family most.”

drill: Your price is too high.

objection: I need to think about it.
means: Something is unresolved, and they don’t want to say what. It might be the product, the payment, the timing or trust in you. “Think about it” is a polite way to leave without conflict.
avoid: “What’s there to think about?” or a fake deadline. Pressure confirms their worry that you care more about the sale than about them.
steps: Give them permission. It takes the pressure off and keeps them talking.
Ask which part needs more thought, and offer two or three options so it’s easy to answer.
Solve that one piece now, or set a specific time to follow up with the answer.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I can appreciate that. It’s a big decision. Can I ask you a couple of questions, so you’ve got everything you need to think it over? When you’re thinking about it tonight, what’s going to come up first: the product, the payment or the timing?”

variants.auto: “I can appreciate that. Is it the vehicle, the payment or the timing? Hey, listen, at the end of the day, all that matters is you get the one you want and enjoy it the way you want to.”
variants.insurance: “Thank you so much for sharing. Is it the coverage, the monthly cost or wanting to talk it over at home? I’ll send you a one-page summary either way.”

drill: I need to think about it.

objection: I need to talk to my spouse first.
means: Often true and smart. Sometimes it’s a softer “no” or a way to buy time. Either way, the decision-maker who isn’t in the room has questions you can answer now.
avoid: Pushing them to decide without their partner, or handing over a card and hoping. The first breaks trust; the second usually ends the deal.
steps: Respect it out loud. It shows you’re on their side.
Ask what their partner will want to know first.
Get them that answer now, and offer to include the partner by phone, video or a quick return visit.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. That’s smart. It’s a decision for both of you. What’s the first thing they’re going to ask you? Let’s get you that answer right now, so you’re not stuck guessing at home.”

variants.auto: “What kind of trips are you two planning in this one? Would she want to see the safety features? Let’s give her a quick FaceTime from right here.”
variants.insurance: “Of course. Would it help if we set 15 minutes when you’re both home? I’ll walk you both through it, so nobody has to explain it secondhand.”

drill: I need to talk to my wife before I decide anything.

objection: I’m just looking.
means: A reflex, not a plan. Most buyers have already researched online and are protecting themselves from a pushy pitch. They want room, not to be ignored.
avoid: “Okay, let me know if you need anything,” then walking away, or launching into a sales pitch. The first loses them; the second proves their fear right.
steps: Agree warmly. Everyone starts there.
Ask about what they’ve already researched or what caught their eye.
Offer one small, useful next step without asking them to commit to anything.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. That’s where everybody starts, and I appreciate you coming in. Can I ask you a couple of questions? What caught your eye when you were looking online, and what matters most to you?”

variants.auto: “That’s where everybody starts. What kind of trips are you planning? What matters most: safety, room or gas mileage? If it’s safety, what would make you feel safer: better headlights, only the driver’s door unlocking, being able to reach help after an accident?”

drill: I’m just looking today.

objection: I can get it cheaper somewhere else.
means: They want the best deal and want you to know they’ve shopped. Sometimes the other offer is real and identical; often it’s different in ways they haven’t noticed.
avoid: Trashing the competitor or claiming they hide fees. It sounds defensive and makes you look like the one with something to hide.
steps: Thank them for shopping. Smart buyers compare.
Ask to see or understand the other offer so you’re comparing the same thing.
Show the differences that matter to them, and be honest if theirs really is better on price.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I really do appreciate that. Can I ask you a couple of questions, to make sure you get the best price wherever you buy? Let’s put the two side by side, apples to apples.”

variants.auto: “I don’t know what that price is, so let’s set it aside. If you buy it online, how will you get it insured and shipped? What’s their policy if it shows up with damage? Are you out your deposit? And how does their warranty compare? I’d be happy to help you look that up.”
variants.insurance: “Glad you’re comparing. Let’s line up the coverage limits and deductibles apples to apples. A lower premium sometimes means less protection when you need it.”

drill: I can get this same thing $1,500 cheaper across town.

objection: Your trade offer is way too low.
means: They’ve looked up a number online, they’re emotionally attached to the vehicle, or they’re focused on the trade instead of the whole deal.
avoid: “That’s what the market says, nothing I can do,” or bumping it $500 to close fast. One ends the conversation; the other trains them to push harder.
steps: Acknowledge that it feels low. Their number came from somewhere.
Walk through how you got your number together: condition, miles, auction data, reconditioning.
Bring the focus back to the difference they’ll pay, not the trade number alone.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. You might be completely right. Would you mind taking a minute so we can make sure it’s in your favor? Let’s say we’d list it at $13,000. Before anyone can buy it, it needs tires and a safety inspection, and it may sit on our lot a couple of months. That’s how we got to $8,000. Do you have anything that shows it’s worth more? If you do, show me, and I’ll take it to my manager.”
drill: Your trade offer is way too low. I looked it up online.

objection: The monthly payment is too high.
means: They like the product but the budget doesn’t fit yet. This is a math problem you can solve together, not a reason to give up.
avoid: Stretching the term without explaining it, or guessing at a number. Surprises later destroy trust and cause cancellations.
steps: Ask what monthly number they’re comfortable with.
Show the levers clearly: down payment, term, coverage or options.
Let them choose. People keep deals they built themselves.
say: “Thank you so much. I can certainly see how you feel. Everything costs more. Can I ask you a couple of questions? What were you paying before? So we’re really talking about the difference. Let’s break it down to the week and the day, and compare apples to apples: gas mileage, safety, what you’re getting.”

variants.auto: “You were paying $580, so we’re talking about $127 more a month. That’s about $29 a week, about four dollars a day. Your old one got 17 miles a gallon, this one gets 20, and you’re getting blind-spot protection you didn’t have. Is that worth about one latte a day to drive the car you want?”
variants.insurance: “Thank you so much for sharing. What monthly amount fits your budget? Let’s see what coverage we can keep at that number, and I’ll tell you plainly what changes.”

drill: That monthly payment is more than I wanted to spend.

objection: I’m not ready to buy today.
means: They may be early in the process, or something is holding them back that they haven’t named. Either way, they’re still talking to you, which is a good sign.
avoid: Fake urgency (“this price is only good today”). Buyers can smell it, and it makes everything else you said sound less true.
steps: Agree that today doesn’t have to be the day.
Ask what would need to be true for them to feel ready.
Set a clear, specific next step: a date, a call or an item to bring back.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I can appreciate that, and I won’t hit you with ‘this price is only good today.’ What would need to be true for you to feel ready? Hey, listen, you realize you have to do something eventually, right? So let’s at least find out where you stand. No pressure. Then you decide.”
drill: I’m not ready to buy today.

objection: Just send me some information.
means: Often a polite brush-off to end the call. Sometimes they genuinely want to review something. The only way to know is to ask what would be useful.
avoid: Emailing a generic brochure and waiting. It almost never gets read, and you lose the conversation.
steps: Say yes. Arguing makes it a fight.
Ask what specifically they want to see so you send the right thing.
Book a short follow-up to go over it together.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I’d be happy to. Can I ask you a couple of questions, so I send you the right thing and not a brochure you’ll toss? What would be most useful to see? And let’s grab ten minutes Thursday to go over it together. Morning or afternoon?”

variants.media: “I’d be happy to. Are you most interested in who sees it, what it costs or results from businesses like yours? I’ll send exactly that and call Thursday to walk you through it.”

drill: Just email me some information and I’ll look at it.

objection: I already have someone for that.
means: They have a relationship and don’t want to feel disloyal. They might be happy, or they might just not have heard a better reason to compare.
avoid: Criticizing their current provider. People defend their choices, especially to a stranger.
steps: Respect the relationship. Loyalty is a good trait in a customer.
Ask what they like most about their current provider.
Offer a no-pressure second opinion, framed around making sure they’re covered or getting the best value.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I really agree with a lot of what you said. Loyalty’s a great thing. What do you like most about working with them? Would you care if I offered a second opinion? Most of the people I help were happy too. If you’re covered, I’ll tell you so.”

variants.insurance: “Glad you have someone you trust. When did they last review your coverage with you? A second look takes 15 minutes, and if your agent has you covered, I’ll tell you so.”

drill: I already have an agent for that.

objection: I’m happy with what I have.
means: No pain right now, so no reason to change. Your job isn’t to invent a problem, it’s to find out if there’s one they haven’t noticed.
avoid: Pushing features. If they don’t feel a need, more features just sound like more cost.
steps: Congratulate them. Happy customers are rare.
Ask one or two questions about what’s changed or what they’d improve if they could.
If nothing comes up, leave the door open and stay in touch.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. That’s great to hear. Can I offer a recommendation? Before you decide you’re all set, if you could change one thing about what you have, what would it be?”
drill: Honestly, I’m happy with what I have.

objection: I don’t have time right now.
means: Usually true. They’re busy and you interrupted. It isn’t a no to what you offer, just to this moment.
avoid: Talking faster to squeeze in your pitch. It confirms you’re ignoring what they just told you.
steps: Respect their time immediately.
Give a one-sentence reason it’s worth a few minutes later.
Ask for a specific time instead of “I’ll call you back.”
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I can appreciate that. I caught you in the middle of something. I’ll be quick: I help businesses like yours get more customers. Is tomorrow at ten or Thursday at two better for five minutes?”
drill: I don’t have time for this right now.

objection: I’ve been burned before.
means: Trust is the real objection. They’re not resisting you, they’re resisting the last person who let them down.
avoid: “We’re not like them.” Everyone says that. Proof works; promises don’t.
steps: Ask what happened, and actually listen.
Acknowledge it plainly. Don’t defend the industry.
Show specifically how you’d prevent that from happening, with something they can check.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing that. I’m sorry that happened. Would you tell me what went wrong? I want to hear your side first, so I can show you exactly how I’d handle it differently, in writing.”

variants.media: “That’s fair. A lot of people have paid for ads that didn’t work. Would you tell me what happened with the last one? Let’s look at what went wrong before we talk about anything new.”

drill: I tried something like this before and got burned.

objection: I want to shop around first.
means: They want to feel confident they made a smart choice. Comparing is how they protect themselves from regret.
avoid: Telling them other places are worse, or trying to keep them from leaving. It reads as fear.
steps: Encourage it. Confident salespeople don’t fear comparison.
Give them a short checklist of what to compare, so your strengths are on it.
Ask permission to follow up after they’ve looked.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Hey, give it a shot. You should. Can I offer a recommendation? Compare apples to apples on three things, not just price: what’s included, what happens if something goes wrong and who you’ll actually deal with. Can I check in Friday to see what you found?”
drill: I want to shop around before I decide.

objection: I can’t afford it right now.
means: Could be a real budget limit, or could mean they don’t see enough value for the cost. Respect it and find out which.
avoid: Making them feel judged or broke. Shame ends conversations for good.
steps: Take it seriously and without judgment.
Ask if it’s the total cost, the monthly amount or the timing.
Offer a smaller starting point if there’s a real fit, or a time to revisit.
say: “Thank you so much for being straight with me. Can I ask you a couple of questions? Is it the total, the monthly amount or just the timing? If there’s a smaller way to start that still helps, I’ll show you. If not, I’ll tell you that too.”

variants.insurance: “Thanks for being honest. Let’s see if there’s a starting amount that protects what matters most, for a number that fits. Even a small policy beats none.”

drill: I just can’t afford it right now.

objection: I don’t need it.
means: They don’t see the problem it solves for them. Either it really isn’t a fit, or they haven’t pictured the situation where it matters.
avoid: Scare tactics. Fear-based pitches feel manipulative, even when the risk is real.
steps: Accept it as possibly true.
Ask a question that helps them picture the situation honestly.
Let them decide, and leave the door open.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. You might be right. Can I ask you a couple of questions? If something happened next month, what would your plan be?”

variants.insurance: “You might be right. If something happened to you tomorrow, how long could your family cover the bills? If the answer is ‘a long time,’ you may not need it, and I’ll tell you so.”

drill: I don’t need life insurance.

objection: Call me back in a few months.
means: Sometimes a real timing issue, like a budget cycle or a lease ending. Often it’s a polite way to end the call.
avoid: “Sure!” and hanging up. A vague callback is a soft no that you agreed to.
steps: Agree, and ask what happens in a few months that makes it a better time.
If the reason is real, book the exact date now.
If it isn’t, ask what would make it worth talking sooner.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Happy to. What changes in a few months that makes it a better time? Let’s put a date on the calendar so I don’t catch you at a bad moment.”
drill: Call me back in a few months.

objection: I don’t want an extended warranty.
means: They’ve heard warranties are a rip-off, or they’re worn out from a long purchase and want to leave. They haven’t weighed the risk for their vehicle and how long they’ll keep it.
avoid: Pressure or scare stories. In F&I, trust is the product, and pushing hard causes cancellations and complaints.
steps: Respect the decision and say it’s their choice.
Ask how long they plan to keep the vehicle and how they’d handle a big repair.
Show the real cost of one common repair compared with the protection, then let them decide.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Totally your call. Can I offer a recommendation? How long do you plan to keep it? Most people keep their car past the factory warranty, so let me show you what one common repair costs next to the coverage, and you decide.”
drill: I don’t want an extended warranty.

objection: Just give me your best price.
means: They want to skip the dance and not feel taken advantage of. Many buyers expect to be lowballed and want to protect themselves.
avoid: Throwing out a number before you know what they want. You’ll negotiate against yourself.
steps: Agree that you’ll be straightforward.
Confirm exactly what they want first, so the price means something.
Give a clear, honest number with what’s included, and explain it.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I appreciate a straight shooter. You wouldn’t buy it until it was the best deal for you anyway, would you? Perfect, we’re on the same page. Let me make sure I’m pricing exactly what you want, so the number is real and not a teaser. Then I’ll walk you through every line.”
drill: Just give me your best price, I don’t have all day.

objection: Advertising doesn’t work for my business.
means: They’ve spent money before without seeing results, or they get most of their business from word of mouth and can’t see where ads fit.
avoid: Arguing with their experience or quoting national statistics. Their own story matters more to them than any chart.
steps: Ask what they tried, and what happened.
Find what was missing: the wrong audience, the wrong message, or no way to measure it.
Propose something small and measurable, tied to how they already win customers.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I really agree with a lot of what you said. A lot of ads don’t work. Can I ask you a couple of questions? What did you try before, who saw it and how did you know if it worked? Most of the time it wasn’t advertising that failed. Let’s find what was missing.”
drill: Advertising doesn’t work for my business. I tried it before.

objection: I'll wait for rates to come down.
means: They're worried about overpaying, and the news keeps telling them rates might drop. Usually the real question is whether the payment works today.
avoid: Predicting where rates are going, or promising they can always refinance. Nobody knows, and a broken promise costs you the customer.
steps: Agree that nobody wants to overpay.
Ask what it costs them to keep their current car running while they wait.
Show the real numbers today, and make sure the loan has no prepayment penalty so refinancing stays an option.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Nobody knows when rates will drop, not me and not the bank. How's your current car holding up while you wait? Let's at least see the real numbers today, then you decide.”
drill: I'm going to wait for interest rates to come down.

objection: I owe more on my car than it's worth.
means: They have negative equity and are embarrassed or worried it kills the deal. They need honesty more than a fast answer.
avoid: Quietly rolling the negative equity into a longer loan without explaining it. It comes back as a cancellation, a bad review or a customer who never returns.
steps: Thank them for being honest.
Lay it out plainly: what they owe, what it's worth, the difference.
Offer real options: more down, a vehicle that keeps the payment healthy, or waiting a few months and coming back.
say: “Thank you so much for being straight with me. A lot of folks are in that spot. Here's what you owe, here's what it's worth, and here's the difference. Let's find the option you can still afford a year from now.”
drill: I owe more on my car than it's worth.

objection: I'll just buy it online and have it delivered.
means: They like the convenience and want to skip the dealership hassle. They often haven't thought about the test drive, the trade or service after the sale.
avoid: Trashing online sellers. It sounds defensive and pushes them toward the screen.
steps: Agree that plenty of people buy online.
Recommend they drive the exact vehicle first.
Give them three questions to ask any seller: trade value, return policy and who services it.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Hey, give it a shot. Before you click buy, drive the one you want, because you can't feel it on a screen. And ask them what they'll give for your trade, what happens if you don't like it, and who works on it later.”
drill: I'll just buy one online and have it delivered.

objection: My rate went up again. I'm shopping around.
means: They feel punished for staying loyal after years of rate increases. They'll leave unless someone shows them they're looking out for them.
avoid: Waiting for them to call, or defending the carrier's increase. By the time they call, they've usually already got another quote.
steps: Call clients before their renewal, not after.
Offer to shop it for them and review coverage, discounts, deductible and bundling.
If you can't beat the price, explain exactly why and what they'd give up to pay less.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. I can certainly see how you feel. I saw your renewal. Before you shop it, let me shop it for you, apples to apples.”
drill: My rate went up again, so I'm shopping around.

objection: I'll just raise my deductible.
means: They want a lower bill and the deductible is the easiest lever they know. It can be smart, or it can leave them stuck after a claim.
avoid: Talking them out of it automatically. For some clients a higher deductible is the right call.
steps: Agree it can be a smart move.
Ask whether they could pay the full deductible tomorrow without strain.
If not, look at other savings first: discounts, bundling and the coverage they carry.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. That can be smart. If you had a claim tomorrow, could you cover a thousand dollars without it hurting? If not, let's look at other ways to save first.”
drill: I'll just raise my deductible to lower my payment.

objection: An app quoted me cheaper.
means: They found a lower number online and want to know if you're overcharging. Often the coverage isn't the same.
avoid: Claiming apps are scams. Some quotes really are cheaper for the same coverage, and they'll trust you more if you admit it.
steps: Thank them for comparing.
Line up limits and deductibles side by side, apples to apples.
Ask who they'll call when they have a claim at night, and be honest if it's truly the same coverage for less.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Let's compare apples to apples, limits and deductibles side by side. And when you have a claim at nine at night, who are you calling: an app, or someone who knows your name?”
drill: An app quoted me cheaper than you.

objection: I'll just run my own Facebook ads.
means: They think doing it themselves saves money. They often haven't counted the hours it takes away from running the business.
avoid: Telling them they'll do it wrong. Owners are proud of what they've built.
steps: Compliment them: they're capable of doing it.
Ask how much time it takes them each week.
Help them weigh that time against what their hour is worth as the owner.
say: “Hey, you're smart enough to do it, thank you for that. How much time does it take you each week? Your hour as the owner is worth a lot. Would it make sense to let someone who does this all day handle it?”
drill: I'll just run my own Facebook ads.

objection: Show me exactly what I'll get back.
means: They've spent money on marketing before without seeing clear results. They want to believe it works but need a reason to.
avoid: Promising a specific number of new customers. Brand and community advertising rarely traces in a straight line, and a broken promise ends the relationship.
steps: Thank them for asking. It's a fair question.
Help them feel what it's like when their name is attached to something joyful in the community.
Be honest that people won't always say how they found you, then show what you can measure.
say: “Thank you for the opportunity to share that with you. When your business is attached to something joyful in your community, people notice. They look you up, read your reviews and learn your story. They may never tell you exactly how they found you, but you'll feel it.”
drill: Show me exactly what I'll get back from this ad.

objection: Nobody reads print anymore.
means: They've heard that digital replaced print and assume their customers don't read magazines. Personal, local content still gets read.
avoid: Arguing print versus digital. It isn't a contest they care about. They care about being seen by local customers.
steps: Ask permission to offer an opinion.
Point out that people keep magazines with their neighbors, kids or church in them.
Show the distribution numbers before they spend anything.
say: “Thank you so much for sharing. Would you care if I offered an opinion? When's the last time you threw away a magazine with someone you know in it? It's about showing up where your neighbors already pay attention.”
drill: Nobody reads print anymore.
